A minister’s wife from Sterling, Massachusetts, Mellen came into Fitz Henry Lane’s world after her brother-in-law took the Universalist pulpit in Gloucester in 1855. By the middle of the decade she was working beside Lane, with free use of his drawings and at times his canvases…

The museum owns Theresa Bernstein’s ⟦0⟧Gloucester in Blue⟦1⟧ (1925), Nell Blaine’s ⟦2⟧Wharf Studio, Gloucester⟦3⟧ (1958) and the archive of the Folly Cove Designers; the Rocky Neck Art Colony also credits it with Martha Walter’s ⟦4⟧Rocky Neck Store and My Studio⟦5⟧ (1920). Ask at the desk which are on view.

In the summer of 1923 Jo Nivison painted ⟦0⟧Church Towers, Gloucester⟦1⟧, a head-on view of this church’s twin towers. It was the summer she and Edward Hopper painted together here, and she encouraged him to take up watercolor. We have not found the painting in a public collection.

Bernstein first came to Gloucester in 1916. She and the painter William Meyerowitz stayed here after their marriage in 1919, and in 1924 bought a house on Mount Pleasant Avenue in East Gloucester (a private home), where they hosted friends including Milton Avery. Both helped found the North Shore Arts Association.

A Philadelphia painter trained under William Merritt Chase, Walter had joined the Gloucester colony by 1913 and kept a studio and gallery on Rocky Neck from the later 1910s into the 1920s. The building is now a gallery.
In 1924 Sally Michel rented the studio next to Milton Avery’s here. They married in 1926, and her work supported the family while he painted.

Blaine rented studios on Rocky Neck in 1954 and 1958; the Whitney’s ⟦0⟧Harbor and Green Cloth, II⟦1⟧ dates from the second summer. From 1974 until her death she summered in East Gloucester. The marker is placed on the avenue; the studio addresses are not published.
Walter’s entries at the Pennsylvania Academy in 1915 included a crowded beach at Bass Rocks; Philadelphia critics praised the Gloucester picture. Parking along Atlantic Road is limited.
Bernstein was still painting this beach around 1980, when she was about ninety: the Brooklyn Museum owns ⟦0⟧Rabbits, Good Harbor Beach, Gloucester⟦1⟧. Summer parking is by fee.
Virginia Lee Burton (1909–1968)
Washington Street (Route 127), Lanesville

The children’s author of ⟦0⟧Mike Mulligan and His Steam Shovel⟦1⟧ taught block printing to her neighbors here and in 1941 founded the Folly Cove Designers, who printed textiles by hand until 1969. Their blocks, fabrics and records are at the Cape Ann Museum.
trails/hopper.html
a downtown walk, then a drive
Hopper came to Gloucester in 1912 with his friend Leon Kroll, and again in the summers of 1923, 1924, 1926 and 1928, mostly painting houses in watercolor. Twelve of his subjects can still be found.
Start here: the museum has the most Hopper context in town, and its docent walks cover the downtown houses.
The church on Church Street. The watercolor is at the Princeton University Art Museum.
A tall yellow Italianate house just up Western Avenue from Stacy Boulevard. The watercolor is at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
On his first visit, in 1912, Hopper painted the fishermen’s houses of the Fort, Gloucester’s Italian neighborhood.
The Second Empire house at the corner of Main and Prospect Streets. The watercolor is at the National Gallery of Art.
Hopper and Jo Nivison, 1923
from Mount Vernon Street
Hopper painted the church’s towers from a distance, from about 15–17 Mount Vernon Street; in the same summer Jo Nivison painted them head-on.
An oil, at the Cincinnati Art Museum

The rail yard by the station gave Hopper ⟦0⟧Freight Cars, Gloucester⟦1⟧, with the steeple of St. Ann’s Church behind the cars; the box factory on Cleveland Street has been torn down. The station is the end of the walk, with trains back to Boston.
2 Clarendon Street, Rocky Neck
The Brooklyn Museum bought this watercolor after its 1923 show. The house was part of Augustus Wonson’s estate.
East Main Street, East Gloucester
Hopper’s 1912 oil of the harbor was painted from the ground above Cripple Cove. The marker is the cove; the exact spot is not recorded.
The point at the end of Good Harbor Beach. The marker is the beach.
trails/rothko.html

In August 2026 Christopher Rothko gave the museum his father’s ⟦0⟧Untitled (wharf, Gloucester, Massachusetts)⟦1⟧ of 1934, the first Rothko in its collection. It shows the salt-fish sheds of the Reed and Gamage wharfs near Smith Cove, painted from Banner Hill.

Avery painted the crowd watching the total solar eclipse of 1932 at Good Harbor. Two years later the friends met here daily: Edith Rothko remembered that they would “go swimming and play handball,” and Rothko painted the game.
Avery first summered in Gloucester in 1921; in 1926 he and the sculptor Leonard Craske rented cottages here, the one record of where he stayed. His ⟦0⟧Gloucester Dawn⟦1⟧ of about 1921 is at Vassar.
The wharfs
Rocky Neck causeway

Smith Cove was the center of Gloucester’s gill-net fishing. Rothko painted its wharfs again and again in 1934: the Reed and Gamage salt-fish sheds with a water tank on the roof, and rows of fish flakes covered with white cloths to keep the sun off the fillets; fishermen among the gill-net reels on a wharf…
The high view
above 186–220 East Main Street

The ridge above Smith Cove, where the Impressionists painted. Rothko painted the Reed and Gamage wharfs from Banner Hill, and Gottlieb sketched them from a similar spot, possibly beside him. The hilltop is private; look from the road.
Rothko, summer 1934

In the summer of 1934 Rothko and his wife, Edith Sachar, rented a house on Calder Street, about half a mile from the wharfs, while the Averys and the Gottliebs summered nearby. The Rothkos arrived first and took the house the Gottliebs had wanted. The house number is not recorded; this is a quiet residential street.
waterfront.html
Fish flakes to draggers
A harbor walk, then a short drive
Leonard Craske’s ⟦0⟧Man at the Wheel⟦1⟧, dedicated August 23, 1925. The plaques list 5,368 men known to have been lost at sea; a single storm in 1862 took 120 men, and storms in 1879 took 159.
At its peak Gorton’s ran dozens of wharves and many flake yards, where cod from the North Atlantic banks was split, salted and dried.
The harbor’s museum of its own working history, on the inner harbor.
The point where Lane painted Ten Pound Island and Hopper painted the fishermen’s houses of the Italian Quarter.
Rothko’s 1934 wharfs had fish flakes on the pier, the last generation of the racks Lane had painted eighty years before.
Low wooden racks on which split, salted cod was laid out in the sun to dry. Whole fields of them appear in Lane’s and later paintings of the waterfront.
Nets hung like a curtain in the water, catching fish by the gills. Mellen’s ⟦0⟧Gloucester Harbor (Laying Nets)⟦1⟧ shows crews setting them.

Small flat-bottomed boats carried on the schooners and rowed out to set lines and nets; Gordon Parks photographed Gloucester crews laying nets by hand from them in 1943. Homer drew boys in dories in 1873.
The fore-and-aft rigged vessels of the Gloucester fleet that brought fish home from the banks.

Lane a native, working there 1840s–1865; Mellen his student in the 1850s
Avery from 1921; Gottlieb and Rothko with him in the 1930s
Motor trawlers that drag a net along the bottom; Emile Gruppé painted them at the wharves.
A berth where a vessel is taken out of the water for repair. Hassam painted one in the 1890s.
A small colonial working boat, the ancestor of many New England fishing craft, among them the Chebacco boat, the dogbody and the pinky.

A heavily built two-masted fishing boat that grew out of the shallop in Chebacco Parish, the part of Ipswich that became the town of Essex in 1819. The name was in use in the second half of the 1700s.
The square-sterned version of the Chebacco boat. Where the name came from is now forgotten.
A schooner-rigged fishing vessel that descended from the Chebacco boat at the end of the 1700s. The name refers to its narrow “pink” stern, from a Dutch word for pinched.
A Chebacco boat converted to a schooner rig by adding a bowsprit and a jib. Gloucester’s fishing timeline records jiggers of 30 tons and more built for mackerel fishing in 1816.

The new fishing schooner of the 1840s: a long hull, a straight keel, sharp bilges and the first hint of a hollow, slicing bow. Lane’s ⟦0⟧Ships in Ice off Ten Pound Island⟦1⟧ shows fishing schooners with the finer hulls of the sharpshooters and clippers.
A fast fishing schooner: sharp-ended, shallow, beamy and over-canvassed. The first clipper owned in Gloucester was built at Essex in 1850; the ⟦0⟧Smuggler⟦1⟧ of 1877 was one.

Dennison J. Lawlor’s design, with an upright stem and a deeper, more stable hull than the clippers. The Fish Commission’s research schooner ⟦0⟧Grampus⟦1⟧, launched in 1885, helped set the new pattern.
Schooners named after their prototype, the ⟦0⟧Fredonia⟦1⟧: a graceful bow, a roomier foredeck and the rounded stern typical of the Gloucesterman.
A schooner with no bowsprit. The first was built in Essex in 1902 to make the work safer for fishermen; Joseph Garland counts the type among the last of the classic Gloucester schooners.
The classic Gloucester fishing schooner of the late 1800s. Built for a hard-fought trade without engines, it was sailed hard, because speed on the voyage home meant success.
A schooner with three masts.
A schooner that fished Georges Bank. Gloucester was using the name by the 1850s.
A schooner that sailed from Gloucester to the Grand Banks of Newfoundland for cod. Kipling’s ⟦0⟧Captains Courageous⟦1⟧ (1897) gives an accurate picture of their life.
A sailing vessel with an engine as well. Gloucester’s first fishing vessel with an auxiliary engine came in 1900, and in the 1920s the fleet began converting to engines, mostly diesel.
Any merchant schooner carrying cargo from one port on the coast to another.
A vessel that carried passengers and higher-value goods between particular ports on a regular schedule. The packet sloops were the most elegant.
A heavily built, undecorated sloop that carried granite blocks from the quarry piers around Cape Ann to other ports.
The New England name for the hermaphrodite brig: square sails on the foremast only, and a spanker and gaff topsail on the main. It was the commonest brig in the coasting trade.
A ship or bark that brought salt to Gloucester for curing fish. Too deep to reach the wharves fully loaded, it was partly unloaded at anchor first.
A small vessel that takes cargo off a deep-loaded ship so that she can reach a wharf. Gloucester did much of this “lightering” in the Stream.

A schooner’s own boat, usually twenty feet long or less, round-bottomed and square-sterned, hung in davits at the stern. It was the lifeboat at sea and carried the captain and crew ashore in port. Lane painted one frozen into the harbor ice.
A boat carried in a schooner’s stern davits and used to bring barrels of rum and molasses out from a beach.
A larger, wider relative of the dory, used for bulky coastal gear such as gill nets and fish traps.
The big rowing boat used in seining. During St. Peter’s Fiesta, crews still race seine boats a half mile out from Pavilion Beach and back.
The long spar at the bow that carries the headsails out over the water. Sailors called it the widow-maker, because men were lost falling from it while tending sail.
On a schooner, the spar along the head of a four-sided sail. In a dory, a gaff was the hook carried for bringing fish aboard.
A schooner has at least two masts: the foremast, nearest the bow, and the mainmast behind it, the taller of the two.
A second spar carried on top of a lower mast, used to fly more sail.
The larger of a schooner’s headsails, set forward of the foremast with the jib.
A headsail flown above and forward of the jib, usually on vessels with a bowsprit.
A small staysail set between the foremast and the mainmast.
The lines that hoist the sails, and the gaffs and booms that hold them.
Lines from the topping lifts to under the boom that catch the sail like a net when it is lowered.
Clumps of frayed rope tied into the rigging so that the sails do not chafe against the lines.
Sails partly lowered or clewed up to dry, as Lane drew them on a half brig in 1851.
Horizontal timbers high on the mast that spread the shrouds.
Small cranes, usually at the stern, for raising and lowering a boat. Banks schooners carried their yawl boats in stern davits.
Holes in the vessel’s sides at deck level that drain water overboard.
Short for forecastle: the crew’s quarters in the forward part of the hull.
The stovepipe of the galley, the ship’s kitchen.
A small cabin on deck that shelters the wheel and the helmsman.
Fishermen’s name for the autopilot, the electrical device that holds a vessel on a set course.
A metal drum with a smooth, curved face, usually mounted on a winch.
The square compartments of the fish hold along the centerline over the keel, between the pens on either side.
Removable dividers of wood or metal that slot into the hold to make pens; when all are in, the hold is “penned up”. Dorymen used smaller ones to section off the dory for fish.
One of the two men who fished from a dory.

Fishing long trawl lines of baited hooks from six to ten dories carried on a schooner. The Gloucester schooner ⟦0⟧Anna⟦1⟧ made a successful dory-trawling trip to the Grand Banks in 1854, but Gloucester was slow to take up the method. Gloucester’s timeline marks 1941 as the year draggers replaced dory fishing.
A long ground line, buoyed and anchored, hung with many short lines of baited hooks. In 1881 a tub of haddock trawl held 500 hooks on about 292 fathoms of line.
A half-barrel holding a coiled trawl and its hooks. In 1881 a dory set out with six to eight of them.
Strips of salted menhaden, the main bait for the winter haddock trawls of 1881; when menhaden ran short, fresh herring took its place. Baiting a tub of 500 hooks took 45 minutes to an hour.
A small iron anchor that holds one end of a trawl to the bottom.
The float marking a trawl: a numbered wooden barrel with a flag. In 1881 each end buoy also carried a black ball.
A hand crank fitted across the bow of a dory to haul in lines heavy with fish.
Doughnut-shaped grips that protected a fisherman’s fingers from the running trawl line. In 1881 each dory carried two pairs, made of wool.
A heavy two-pronged wooden stick for stunning fish and taking hooks from their throats.
A heavy wooden club for stunning or killing big fish such as halibut, which can weigh more than 200 pounds.
A wooden or metal scoop for throwing water out of the dory.
Narrow wooden pegs set in a dory’s rail that hold the oars in place while rowing.
Dorymen carried a fog horn and a kerosene lamp to signal the schooner, by sound or by light, in thick fog or darkness.
The dory’s narrow, V-shaped stern board.
To feed a line over the side, hand over hand.
Fishing with a single line carrying one or two hooks. Dory trawling, with many hooks on one line, later replaced it.
A metal rod that held the two hooks of a Georges Bank hand line 12 to 18 inches apart.
The top boat, or the top fisherman, of the fleet. The word goes back to fishing from the deck, when the best fisherman held the highest place in the bow.
A net about 1,000 feet long set in a circle around a school of mackerel. It replaced hand-lining for mackerel; Gloucester’s timeline dates it to 1848.
A net towed along the bottom and held open by two otter doors. Its arrival in 1905 changed fishing on the New England banks.
The bottom and top lines of a trawl net. Floats of metal, plastic or glass on the headrope hold the mouth of the net open.
The cables from a trawler’s winches to the two sides of the net, which carry the pull of the boat to the trawl.
Fishermen’s short name for Georges Bank. The Fish Commission’s reports from Gloucester in 1883 list the cod and halibut landed “from George’s Bank” month by month.
The great fishing banks off Newfoundland, where Gloucester’s salt bankers went for cod.
A vessel’s catch as landed. A report from Gloucester in December 1883 notes that the vessels from Georges Bank “all brought in good fares of cod”.
Both the voyage and the fish it brings home: the whole catch aboard is “the trip”.
The passage from the fishing grounds back to the home port.
Fishing near home in small vessels and boats. In November 1883 Gloucester’s shore fisheries had 56 vessels and 448 men.
Fish that live near the bottom, such as cod and haddock, the mainstay of the New England fisheries.

Packing fish in ice instead of salt became common about 1845, so that fresh fish could reach market. With faster schooners and the railroad, it revived Gloucester’s fishing. The ice was cut from fresh-water ponds.
Clarence Birdseye’s quick-freezing method, which in 1924 started the processing of frozen fish.
A baited trap set on the bottom, one of the traps of the coastal fisheries in Lane’s time. Homer painted three boys in a dory with lobster pots in 1875.
A field of fish flakes beside the wharves. Lane’s 1836 view of Gloucester shows the Wonson family’s flake yard in East Gloucester, and Five Pound Island later became one.
The crew that cleaned cod on deck: the throater cut down the belly and took off the head, the gutter removed the insides but saved the liver, and the splitter took out the backbone.
The slime, blood and fluids spilled when fish are dressed. Schooners kept a gurry pen on deck.
A salt cure that used more salt than dunfish but less than pickled “green” cod.

Cod quickly dried and lightly salted, sometimes cured in dark rooms for two or three months under salt hay or eelgrass and weights. The name belongs to the small-boat fisheries of eastern Maine and the Bay of Fundy.
Cod pickled in casks of brine rather than dried; the cure took more salt than kenching.
Fishermen cut the tongue out of each cod they hauled aboard to keep count of their catch before the fish was salted.
A federal payment that helped Gloucester fishermen rebuild their fleet after independence.
Gloucester’s trade with Surinam, on the north coast of South America, was under way by 1790 and paid for many of the town’s merchant vessels and wharves until it collapsed in 1863.
A dock worker who unloads vessels in Gloucester Harbor.
The Jodrey State Fish Pier, opened in 1938 and named for Everett R. Jodrey.
A wharf built on cribs, rectangular frames of timber that look like a log cabin, filled in, with beams laid over the top crib to carry the deck.
A pier of piles and timber filled in with rocks. Gloucester built finger piers and bulkheads this way.
Gloucester’s word for the pilings driven along a wharf as fenders where vessels tie up.
Wharf space in Gloucester Harbor was scarce, so coasting vessels moored together and passed cargo to smaller craft that carried it to nearby towns, and the reverse.
The wide channel at the entrance to the Inner Harbor, where vessels anchored while they waited to unload, often lightering there first.

A cradle on rails that hauls a vessel out of the water for repair. The Rocky Neck railways, begun in 1859 and worked by a steam engine until about 1970, are said to be the oldest still operating in the country.

The Blynman Canal, dug in 1643 between the harbor and the Annisquam River so that small vessels could avoid the passage around Cape Ann. Storms filled it with sand in 1704 and 1723; it was reopened in 1823.
The breakwater at Eastern Point that has kept southerly swells out of the harbor since 1905. Stay off it when it is wet or icy.
A small island in the harbor, once fit only for sheep pounds, that later became a flake yard for drying fish.

Many Gloucester schooners came from the shipyards on the Essex River. The first knockabout was built in Essex in 1902 and the ⟦0⟧Adventure⟦1⟧ in 1926; Arthur D. Story launched the ⟦2⟧Gertrude L. Thebaud⟦3⟧ there in 1930.
The formal word for the share system, under which the money from a trip is divided between the boat and the crew.
Adding up the trip’s bills and working out each man’s share and the boat’s; the balance sheet is the settlement.
The gross stock is all the money the boat and crew earned from a trip; the net stock is what is left after the bills charged against it are taken out.
When a trip earned less than its expenses, the crew went in the hole and paid the bills from their own pockets. The deficit was the hole bill.
The crewman elected to speak for the crew when the settlement is made.
An East Coast word for a berth on a fishing boat, or the promise of one.
A snack between meals: a cup of coffee and a sandwich.
A wide-brimmed, waterproof oiled hat for foul weather.
Cloth tubes worn on the forearms and held by a thumb loop. They keep the arms warm and wash clean of slime and blood more easily than sleeves.
A small bag for carrying and stowing a sailor’s personal things.

Gloucester’s June festival for St. Peter, patron saint of fishermen, first held in 1926 and put on by the Italian-American community: an open-air Mass, processions, seine-boat races, the greasy pole and the blessing of the fleet.

A heavily greased pole run out over the harbor with a flag at the end, which walkers try to grab before they fall in. It was added to the Fiesta in 1931, after a contest in Terrasini, Sicily, the home town of many Gloucester families.
“Long live St. Peter!” The cry is shouted in the Fiesta processions and by the greasy-pole walkers.

On Fiesta Sunday a priest reads out the names of Gloucester’s fishing boats and blesses them. Gloucester’s timeline dates the first blessing to 1945. In 1957 the Portuguese and Italian fleets were blessed on separate Sundays; by 1977 the two communities celebrated together.
Each August a procession goes to the Man at the Wheel, where families lay oars and wreaths and cast flowers into the harbor for the men lost at sea.
The plaques beside the Man at the Wheel bearing the names of Gloucester fishermen lost at sea, more than 5,000 of them. New names are still added.
Leonard Craske’s bronze helmsman on Stacy Boulevard, dedicated in 1925, with the line from Psalm 107, “They that go down to the sea in ships”.
The church of Gloucester’s Portuguese community, modeled on Santa Maria Madalena in the Azores. Between its towers a statue of Mary holds a two-masted schooner.
The memorial near the Man at the Wheel that honors the women whose faith kept fishing families going.

Races between fishing schooners of Gloucester and Nova Scotia, begun in 1920. Lunenburg’s ⟦0⟧Bluenose⟦1⟧ never lost a series. The last, sailed off Gloucester and Boston in October 1938 against the ⟦2⟧Gertrude L. Thebaud⟦3⟧, was the final race between North Atlantic sailing fishing schooners.
